summary: Apollos is a Mars exploration planning prototype using NASA and USGS data across eight mission regions. It helps users plan routes, mark no-go areas, estimate travel and return times, and record discoveries with photos. Jezero supports measured terrain routing; other regions use manual routes with simulated travel.
details:
Apollos is a Mars surface-exploration planning prototype that brings scientific objectives, route planning, and field discoveries into one workspace. It uses NASA and USGS resources to help users explore eight mission regions: Perseverance, Curiosity, Pathfinder, Phoenix, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, and Viking 1.

What it does and how it works

Users choose a mission and scientific objective, examine imagery and supporting evidence, and plan a journey from a proposed base to a destination. They can mark no-go areas, estimate travel time, review their return budget, and rehearse the trip through simulated movement.

Within a measured area of Jezero Crater, Apollos calculates candidate routes using a USGS elevation model, avoiding unknown terrain cells, slopes above the selected limit, and user-entered exclusions. Other regions support manual routes with detour waypoints and exclusion checks.

During a simulated traverse, users can record discoveries, attach photographs, and save observations at their simulated position. Records remain in the browser and can be exported for sharing. Adaptive distance rings and a scale bar use a source-verified Mars reference model.

Benefits and intended impact

Apollos connects why a location matters scientifically with what needs to be considered before travelling there. Its guided workflow encourages users to examine evidence, account for the return journey, identify uncertainties, and document findings.

Our intended impact is to make Mars mission planning more understandable and accessible while demonstrating how exploration tools could connect preparation and fieldwork. It is a research and educational prototype—not operational astronaut guidance.

Tools and technologies

We developed Apollos using:

  • React and TypeScript for the interface.
  • OpenLayers for interactive maps and overlays.
  • JavaScript for routing, distance calculations, budgets, and storage.
  • Vite, Node.js, and npm for development, builds, and testing.
  • Python, NumPy, and tifffile to extract the Jezero terrain data.
  • Git and GitHub for team collaboration, and Prettier for consistent formatting.

The app runs in a web browser without specialized hardware. Its resources include JPL Mars Trek imagery, USGS geological and terrain data, NASA mission records, Curiosity route imagery, and Perseverance raw images. NASA Worldview informed map interaction ideas; its Earth imagery does not feed Mars calculations.

What makes it creative

Apollos combines a mission atlas, a guided planning process, and a field notebook. Users move through Objective → Plan → Review → Traverse, keeping scientific purpose connected to travel decisions and observations.

It also distinguishes measured evidence from assumptions. Instead of presenting every route as safe, it shows what the available data supports and what remains unknown.

Factors our team considered

We considered astronaut safety, scientific relevance, usability, data quality, and teamwork. This included slope constraints, exclusion areas, travel duration, return reserves, source attribution, and the limitations of coarse terrain data.

We also preserved each teammate’s mission contributions within a shared workflow. Remaining limitations—such as unverified obstacle clearance, demonstration endurance assumptions, browser-only storage, and the absence of live Mars tracking—are made explicit.
